Image tags and distribution package names are examples; before using them, confirm that the images are still supported, the repositories are available, and your installed version matches your needs. The examples have not been tested by running them.
This article explains how to install Distrobox and its dependencies on Linux, complete the initial setup, and choose a suitable container backend for different use cases.
Distrobox itself is a collection of shell scripts with no dependency on a particular runtime. However, it requires at least one working container manager to create and run containers.
Distrobox supports three backends, with the following minimum version requirements:
Runs as an ordinary user, reducing host privileges; shared HOME still carries risks
A rootful backend has host privileges; guest user identities and file ownership also depend on mappings
Lightweight alternative; check specific features against the version

Podman's rootless mode suits user-level environments. Distrobox configures the guest user and UID mappings to reduce file ownership conflicts. Docker also supports rootless mode; the backend type alone does not determine the identity of every guest process. Regardless of the backend, sharing HOME allows container programs to modify the host user's files.

1.3 Verifying Rootless Configuration (Required for Podman Users)
Podman's rootless mode relies on /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid to allocate subordinate UID/GID ranges to the current user. Check whether the current user is configured:

If there is no output, rootless mode is not configured. Here is an example of manual allocation (requires sudo; first inspect every user's existing ranges. The example range must be unused and nonoverlapping. On NixOS, use declarative configuration instead of manually editing generated files):

After changing mappings, stop the affected containers first, then follow the Podman documentation to use podman system migrate to update the rootless pause process. This affects the current user's containers; it is not simply restarting some required daemon.

How Rootless Works: For a detailed explanation and troubleshooting, see Podman Rootless Containers. In brief, the host allocates nonoverlapping subordinate UID/GID ranges to map multiple guest identities. The specific mapping of UID 0 depends on the user namespace configuration; Distrobox's keep-id differs from ordinary Podman's default mapping.
Distrobox offers three installation methods, listed below in order of preference.
The following are common package-manager installation methods. Confirm repository branches, package versions, and minimum supported distribution releases for your current distribution:
Repository location varies by distribution; consult the current package database
Official compatibility documentation lists inclusion in the default repositories from 22.10 onward; check other sources for older releases
NixOS Users: Interactions between Distrobox and the Nix environment require special care on NixOS. See Part 06: NixOS and Declarative Containers in this series.
Advantages of installing with a package manager:
The distribution can handle packaging dependencies; you still need to check that a working Podman, Docker, or Lilipod backend is available
Files are installed to distribution-managed paths, usually in the Nix store and profiles on NixOS
Useful when you do not want to use a package manager or need to install to a nonstandard location, such as a user directory without sudo access:

This 1.8.2.5 installer has version=1.8.2.5 built in and downloads the corresponding tag unless --next is used. Alternatively, check out a tag as described in the next section and install from the local source directory.
Specify the installation prefix. Scripts go into <path>/bin/; documentation, completions, and icons follow the installer's layout
Install the latest development version from the git main branch (not a stable release)
The 1.8.2.5 installer has no --version parameter; pin the version through a source checkout
Copies the main distrobox program and helper scripts (distrobox-create, distrobox-enter, distrobox-list, etc.) into <prefix>/bin/
Installs default configuration and documentation according to the version and distribution packaging; do not assume there is always a distrobox.conf listing every option

Limitations of the Installation Script: The script does not resolve dependencies or install podman or docker. If you do not already have a container backend, consult the Podman installation guide or use your distribution's repository to install podman first.

After manual installation, manage PATH yourself: ensure <prefix>/bin/ is in your $PATH. If you use ~/.local/bin, most modern distributions already include this path in their shell configuration.

3.2 Ways to Specify the Container Manager

Distrobox scripts first load installation/system/user configuration, then apply supported environment variables. Available CLI options subsequently override the corresponding settings. Select the backend with DBX_CONTAINER_MANAGER or the container_manager configuration setting; create/enter in 1.8.2.5 has no --container-manager option.
Method One: An Environment Variable for One Invocation
Podman and Docker maintain separate container stores. Subsequent operations must use the backend that created the container; do not assume containers are found automatically across backends.
Method Two: A Session-Level Environment Variable
Method Three: A Configuration File (Persistent, Recommended)

Configuration files use shell syntax and are sourced by the scripts, so they can execute commands; load only trusted configuration. The location of installation defaults depends on the prefix or Nix store. Check the current scripts for the override order of system files, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/distrobox/distrobox.conf, and ~/.distroboxrc.
When multiple backends coexist, set container_manager="podman" as the default and use DBX_CONTAINER_MANAGER=docker distrobox ... for a one-off switch. Switching backends does not migrate containers.

4.3 Enter the Container and Verify It
After entering, you will notice that the shell prompt changes (by default, it gains a container-name prefix). Run the following checks inside the container:
GUI Application Does Not Appear: If xeyes or glxgears reports cannot open display, X11/Wayland forwarding is not working. Check the following:
On the host, confirm that echo $DISPLAY or echo $WAYLAND_DISPLAY has a value
Check that /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid are configured correctly (see Section 1.3)
Try exiting and re-entering: run exit, then distrobox enter test
After verification, remove the test container:
distrobox version prints a version number
distrobox create successfully pulls an image and creates a container
distrobox enter successfully opens the container shell
$HOME inside the container matches the host
<input disabled="" type="checkbox"> Packages can be installed and managed inside the container
<input disabled="" type="checkbox"> GUI applications display correctly (optional; depends on display forwarding configuration)
